Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

since conjunction

from the time when

also ever since, it’s been … since, for (so long), since when?

classical

Liv. 40.5: ex quō obses Rōmae fuit (Lewis & Short)
Traupman 182: Ex quō tempore …?, since when …?

ex quō (tempore)

relative phrase, with the indicative

since, ever since

“From the time when”. For a time that runs on into the present, Latin uses the present with jam where English says “have been”: jam diū ignōrō, “I have not known for a long time”.

Other words

  • cum (with a length of time) — since (it is so long since)

    conjunction, with the indicative: annī sunt octō cum … · also used · classical · Cic. Clu. 82: annī sunt octō cum ista causa in istā meditātiōne versātur (Lewis & Short); Plaut. Aul. prol. 4: hanc domum jam multōs annōs est quom possideō (Lewis & Short)

    “It is eight years since …”, with the present when the thing still goes on.

  • jam (+ present) — have been (doing) since, for

    adverb with the present tense · also used · classical · Cic. Fam. 7.9.1: jam diū ignōrō quid agās

    The usual Latin for “I have been … for so long”.

Examples

  • ex quō obses Rōmae fuit

    ever since he was a hostage in RomeLiv. 40.5 (Lewis & Short)

  • hanc domum jam multōs annōs est quom possideō

    it is many years now that I have owned this housePlaut. Aul. prol. 4 (Lewis & Short)

  • jam diū ignōrō quid agās; nihil enim scrībis

    I haven’t known for a long time how you are, for you never writeCic. Fam. 7.9.1

  • Ex quō tempore fuistī ōrnātū mīlitārī?

    Since when have you been in uniform?Traupman 182

  • ūsque ab (+ abl.)

    ever sinceTraupman 379

See also when, already.
